title: Gurdwaras abroad
hookLine: great gurdwaras stand in London, Toronto, Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur

lines: THE SAME THING AT THE CENTER.
cards: Where does a Guru live when the family moves across the world? Try a wet London street, buses going by, and then a building with a dome and a tall saffron flag out front.

A wide suburban road outside Toronto, a parking lot full on a Sunday morning. A gurdwara in Nairobi, its doors open to the morning traffic. One in Kuala Lumpur, shoes lined up at the door in the heat.
Different weather, different streets, and inside each one the same thing at the center: the Guru Granth Sahib, on a raised seat, under a canopy.

teach.h: WHERE THE GRANTH SITS, THE GURU SITS.
teach.b: First, what makes a gurdwara. It isn't the dome or the city.
Sikhs say the Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru, so wherever it is installed with respect, on a raised seat, opened each morning and put to rest at night, that place is the Guru's court, the darbar.
A gurdwara in Toronto is not a copy of one in Punjab. It's the same Guru, in a new place. Second, the Guru's word on this.

Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, writes, in paraphrase: wherever my True Guru goes and sits, that place is beautiful. Some Sikhs far from Punjab hear their own story in that line. The Guru goes where the sangat goes.
Third, two signs you can spot from the street.
The Nishan Sahib, the tall flag, marks a gurdwara from a distance. The langar marks it from inside: a free kitchen where anyone may sit and eat, Sikh or not. Those two travel well.
Fourth, what else grew in these buildings.

teach.h: MORE THAN A PLACE TO PRAY.
teach.b: For families who moved far from home, the gurdwara became more than a place to pray.
It's where weddings happen, where children learn Gurmukhi letters on weekends, where newcomers find someone who speaks their language, and where a stranger can get a hot meal.
In London, Toronto, Nairobi and Kuala Lumpur the details differ: the food, the accents, the weather at the door. The seat at the center is the same.

how: Sikhs around the world gather at local gurdwaras, where the Guru Granth Sahib is installed, kirtan is sung, and the langar serves a free meal to anyone who comes.

o: Sikh houses of the Guru far from Punjab, the same Guru anywhere

o: the Guru stays only in Punjab.
wherever the True Guru goes and sits, that place is beautiful.
only a large building can hold the Guru.
games.why: Guru Ram Das writes that wherever the True Guru goes and sits, that place is beautiful. some Sikhs far from home hear their own story in it.

practice: Picture the streets of the town where you live, or one you love, and somewhere among them, maybe, a saffron flag you've walked past without noticing.
Picture the door, the shoes lined up, the smell of the kitchen, and the raised seat at the center, and rest there for a few breaths, with Waheguru if you pray.

wordCard.voice: Gurdwaras abroad. Sikh houses of the Guru far from Punjab, in London, Toronto, Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur and beyond, each one the Guru's court because the Guru Granth Sahib is there. Today's word.
